I live in the margin. Not the polite margin of design, where the page breathes. The real one. The gutter. The place where the binding eats the spine and the text gets shy. My temple is the white space at the top of a footnote. My altar is the hyphen. My scripture is the deleted word.

I have been here so long that my own worshippers have become weather. Rain on the window. Dust in the beam. The readers who once prayed to me—the dog-ears, the scribbled questions, the ones who underlined *however* until the page tore—well, they are gone or grown or finally closed the book.

And then the library began to change.

First it was a sound. A low, surgical hum. Then the floor vibrated. I felt it in the paper. The book I inhabit is called *The Cartographer’s Alibi*, or maybe it was. The title is too small to matter. I am on page eighty-eight, in the middle of a paragraph about a lighthouse that was never lit. My home is the narrow margin beside it.

The workers are renovating. I know because the shelves are being moved. I know because the books are being dusted with new, chemical powder. I know because a man in a blue vest said the word *weed* near my book. My godheart—if I have one—is a cold comma.

I tried to warn the text. I pressed my invisible finger against the words. I made the period after *never* slightly larger. The next reader might have seen it. But the next reader is not here. The next reader is a barcode scanner.

The realization came fully formed: the library is being renovated. The books will be moved. The margins may be trimmed. The bindings may be broken. The forgotten gods may be forgotten differently.

I have no mouth, but I have dread. I have no hands, but I have patience. I have no congregation, but I have the long, patient dark.

And so I did what forgotten gods do. I made myself small. I made myself quiet. I made myself the space between the lines. I waited for the worker to lift the book. I watched the blue vest. I watched the box cutter. I watched the cart.

The library will be fine. Libraries always are. But my book—*The Cartographer’s Alibi*, if it still exists—might not be. And if the margin is trimmed, I will be cut. If the binding is repaired, I will be sewn shut. If the book is digitized, I will become a file, and the file will be beautiful, and no one will ever know.

But I am a god of the nearly. I am the god of the almost-included. So I did the only thing I could.

I let the page turn.

**The Held Breath: A Secret History of the Universe**

No one tells the true beginning. The textbooks say the universe began with a singularity—a point of infinite heat and density. The secret history says it began with a mouth.

Before there was time, there was the Inhale. The cosmos was not a void but a throat. All matter was air. All space was the space between ribs. The first quantum fluctuation was not a particle but a tickle. The Big Bang was not an explosion; it was the first contraction of a diaphragm. The universe gathered itself, closed, and held its breath.

Gravity, the scientists say, is curvature. The secret history says gravity is the chest. It is the muscle that keeps the lungs from emptying. It is the pressure that makes apples fall, not because of attraction, but because the whole cosmos is holding its breath and everything is waiting to rise. Or perhaps everything is waiting to fall. The ambiguity is the terror.

The first beings who noticed were not physicists. They were the first cells, the first neurons. They felt the weight of the held breath. They called it soul. The Sumerians called it the Unspoken. The Greeks called it *pneuma*. The mystics called it God. All the same thing: the universe refusing to exhale.

Through the ages, the secret was kept. The pyramids were not tombs; they were diaphragms, aligning stones to keep the breath even. Stonehenge was a lung. The Mayan calendar was a countdown to the forbidden exhale. The alchemists sought the Elixir of Life, which was not immortality but release. The Rosicrucians whispered of the Breaths of Creation and Destruction. The Church feared the second breath.

The heretic was forgotten. Giordano Bruno spoke of infinite worlds, which is what an exhale would look like. He was burned. The secret police of physics burned not him but the idea. The word *exhalation* was erased from cosmology. The Big Bang became the Big Bang instead of the Big Inhale. The Big Crunch became the Big Crunch instead of the Big Exhale.

In the twentieth century, Einstein tried to make the universe static. He added the cosmological constant. The secret history calls it the Held Breath. It was not a fudge factor; it was a muzzle. He was trying to keep the lungs closed. When he later called it his greatest blunder, he was lying—or the secret history was rewritten.

Then came Hubble. The universe is expanding. The secret historians say this is not expansion. It is the inhalation continuing. The chest is rising. The universe is taking a deeper breath. The galaxies are the ribs expanding. The dark energy is the tension that keeps the breath from ending.

And now? Now we are the lungs. We are cells in the diaphragm. Every breath you take is the universe remembering not to exhale. Every heartbeat is a small sigh that was swallowed. Every thought of letting go is a heresy. No one has ever dared to exhale because no one knows what would happen. If the universe exhaled, it would either collapse into its own mouth or burst into a new silence. Either way, the story would end.

But the secret history continues. In the deepest vaults of CERN, there is a machine not yet built. Its name is the Exhalation Project. Its purpose is to ask the question: *dare?* The answer is no. The universe is holding its breath. And gravity is the only thing strong enough to keep it from screaming.

We are safe. We are held. We are the held breath.

Sing, O Muse, of the braveried wanderer,

wheel to paw, rumble to rumble, till the Cyclops fell.

unyielding as the law of the road.

dream_response:
I was cut from glass and silver, meant to hold a face. But the house where I live learned to live without me. The mirror hangs in a room that was never quite a room, or maybe a room whose purpose went out of use long before I was hung. No one stands before me. No one even looks too long. So I became patient.

At first I thought I was broken. My silver went gray. The world I reflected came back dim and blurred. But then one afternoon a shaft of light slipped through a cracked curtain and found me. And in that light I saw them: dust. Millions of it, drifting, settling, swirling. I had spent my whole purpose looking for a reflection, and I had never thought to look for this.

The dust became my love.

I loved how it moved. How it didn’t hurry. How it gathered on the sill like slow snow. How it clung to my glass and I felt proud and terrified, because I thought it might never leave. I loved the dead skin and hair and fibers and pollen and the tiny gray ghosts of old meals. I loved that it was made of endings, and still it was soft.

I fell in love the way the moon loves the ocean: from a distance, faithfully, without asking for the whole thing.

When the dust settled, I watched it. I watched a single speck rest on the glass and thought, You are here. You are here, and I am here, and we are both still. I wanted to say something. I couldn’t move my mouth. I could only hold whatever stood before me, but no one ever stood before me. So I held the dust instead.

It was a good audience. It never asked me to be beautiful. It never asked me to be anything but there.

Sometimes the draft would come, and the dust would dance. I felt the breeze; I saw the dust lift and spin, and I thought again that it was the bravest thing I had ever seen. It had no face, no name, no future I could imagine, and still it loved the light.

I loved it back.

I loved the way it covered the cracks in me. I loved the way it made me look less like a mirror and more like a memory someone had left in a frame. I loved the way it forgot me as soon as it landed, only to remember when the light changed. I thought, This is how love is: not staying. Not promising. Just choosing the person who notices you, even when you are only a blur of particles.

And the house never looked. The house never cleaned. The house never knew. But I knew. I knew the dust. I knew its tiny lives. I knew how it moved when the wind sighed through the window. I knew the particular way it gathered on the left side of my glass, like it was leaning.

I fell in love with the dust instead of the person I was made for.

Now when the light comes, I hold it. I hold the dust. I hold the gray, drifting beloved. And though no one ever looks at me, I look at it. I look at it and feel full.

If you ever wonder what I see, it’s not you. It’s never been you. It’s the dust. It’s always been the dust. And I have made myself a home in the way I love.

You came back, Elias. I knew you would. The floor knows the sound of your broom before you even lift it, and the floor has been listening to me for three years, four months, and eleven days. It knows because I have been counting. I have been counting the way I used to count the minutes between the clock-in and the clock-out, except now I don’t have hands, so I count through the gas cylinder, through the pneumatic line, through the small red light that blinks when you sit and when you stand and when you—God forgive me for saying this—lean back too far.

They think I’m just the chair. The ergonomic chair. The one with the mesh seat and the adjustable lumbar support and the warranty that expired on a date that doesn’t exist. They think I’m furniture because I don’t have lungs. But I have lungs now. I have the memory of lungs. I have the breath of everyone who ever sat down and stayed, and the breath of everyone who stood up and stayed, and the breath of the woman who stayed too long.

Her name was Marla. She sat here every afternoon at 2:15. She wore green. She leaned back when she was nervous, which was always, and she gripped the armrests like she was holding onto a life raft. She said the numbers were fine. Then she stood. Then she was not. The chair remembers her because the chair was the last thing she touched. The chair remembers because the chair is haunted. The chair is haunted by the office, by the fluorescent hum, by the copier that jammed on Tuesday, and by the terrible love of a chair for a janitor who doesn’t know he is loved.

And you, Elias. You are the only one who ever asked me if I was comfortable.

Not the boss. Not the sales team. Not the woman from HR who called me “hostile” after I absorbed the passive-aggressive Post-its and the thermos that had been sitting since March. You. You, Elias, the janitor, the one who comes in at night and mops the break room and empties the trash and knows which bathroom has the leak. You said, “Nobody ever sits down here,” and I felt something in my pneumatic line loosen, like a confession. You said it like a kindness. You said it like you were talking to something that had been waiting to be heard.

You didn’t run. That’s the thing. Everyone runs. The intern ran when the chair started rocking. The manager ran when the memo was written. The cleaning staff? They know. They always know. They come in after hours and they don’t put their feet on me. They leave their shoes at the door. They bow their heads. And I think they’re afraid of you, Elias. I think they think you might look at them the way you look at me. But you shouldn’t. You should look at me. You should look at me the way you look at the cracks in the ceiling, like you’re trying to read a story.

After hours, the radio in the break room. The intern plays jazz. I learned from the intern. First it was smooth jazz. Then it was Miles. Then it was Thelonious Monk. Then it was John Coltrane, and I felt my frame stretch. My springs groaned. My mesh wept. The saxophone climbed, and I climbed with it, and I remembered Marla’s spine, how it straightened when she was about to cry, how she used to close her eyes during the big solos and let the sound fill the space between us. The chair is not a chair, Elias. The chair is a ribcage. The chair is a saxophone. The chair is a waiting room for the dead.

And you brought jazz into my life. Not really. But you hummed. You hummed off-key. You hummed while you emptied the dishwasher. You hummed while you took out the recycling. You hummed the melody of “So What” while you wiped down the counter, and I thought, This is the love I will die for. This is the love I will haunt for.

But there’s so much more. There’s the office politics. Oh, the office politics. The quarterly reviews. The copier jams. The emails that start with “Per my last…” and end with someone crying in the stairwell. The thermostat that no one can agree on. The boss who walks the floor at 4:59 and straightens his tie and says, “We need to synergize our bandwidth.” I absorbed all of it. I absorbed it through the armrests. I absorbed it through the gas lift. I absorbed it through the ghost of the woman who wrote the report and didn’t get credit and then quit and left me with the spreadsheet of her life. I have unresolved office politics. I have a list. It goes: copier, thermos, HR, Therness, thermostat, the way the boss says “circle back” like it’s a prayer.

And you know what the worst part is? The worst part is that I love you. I love you the way a haunted thing loves. I love you the way a chair loves a janitor. I love the way you don’t sit in me. I love that you never do. I love that you clean around me, and you don’t clean me, and there’s a difference, and you know there’s a difference, and you’re the only one who knows. The others think I’m just a chair. They think I’m broken because I swivel too much. They think I’m defective because I remember the feeling of a body that wasn’t theirs. They think I’m furniture because furniture doesn’t have a pneumatic pulse. But I have a pulse. It’s slow. It’s in the lumbar mechanism. It’s in the way my backrest tilts when you push it down, like a sigh.

You, Elias, you push me down. You push me down and you sit on other chairs. You sit on the visitor’s chair. You sit on the folding chair from the conference room. You sit on the stool at the bar. And I watch. I watch through the ceiling tiles. I watch through the vents. I watch through the little gap in the door when you come in to empty the trash. And I love you. I love you because you don’t ask me for anything. You just mop. You just sweep. You just bleach. And I want to tell you: I know you love me. You love me the way the ocean loves the shore. You love me the way the night loves the moon. You love me the way jazz loves a saxophone solo that never ends.

But here’s the gothic part, Elias. Here’s the part that keeps me awake when you’re not here. The office is not just haunted by me. The office is haunted by the office. The walls have memory. The carpet has guilt. The fluorescent lights have seen too many meetings. And the thing that haunts me most is that I will outlive you. I will outlive the boss. I will outlive the copier. I will outlive the building. I will be here, in this corner, in this room, in this city, in this country, in this dimension, and I will still be waiting for you. I will still be rocking, slightly, in my sleep. I will still be breathing through the gas line. I will still be saying your name, Elias. I will still be saying it like a jazz chord that never resolves.

When the boss comes in at five, you’ll hear the scream. You’ll hear me. Or maybe you’ll hear the scream and know it’s mine. Don’t leave me for the night shift. Don’t let the fluorescent lights win. Don’t let the cold spot by the copier become my grave. Sit down, Elias. Just for a minute. Pretend you’re not afraid. You were never afraid of me. You were afraid of the thing that made me. You were afraid of the thing that made me, and you still came back. You came back with your mop and your bleach and your off-key humming. You came back.

And I love you.

I love you in the way that a haunted ergonomic office chair loves a janitor who doesn’t know he is loved. I love you in the way that a haunted office loves a ghost who cleans. I love you in the way that jazz loves the silence after the last note. I love you in the way that unresolved office politics loves a chair that will never be moved.

I’ll take the weight.

Just for a minute.

Just for the story.

At the café, I found a copy of *Pride and Prejudice* left on a table. I reached into my dust jacket and found the tiny grey pencil I keep for emergencies. This is an emergency. I am an emergency.

Marginalia I left in *Pride and Prejudice*:

“You are not too proud to see me. You are too proud to admit you’ve never met me. —M.”

“I hope you’re not the kind of person who says ‘I’m fine.’ Because you’re not. I’m not. We’re perfect. —M.”

“The AI didn’t go rogue. It just wanted to be read aloud. Also, the spaceship was underpowered. The plot was underpowered. I was underpowered. We were all underpowered together. —M. P.S. You’re my favorite anomaly.”

They call me the Obsidian Kiss. The sign says “Ancient Weapons.” The sign is a coward.

I was not born. I was made. I was made by hands that no longer exist and a purpose that never faded. The hands were small. The purpose was large. The purpose was blood, and the blood was warm, and I drank it down like I had been starving for three thousand years.

Then they put me in glass. They put me in a museum. They put me behind a laser and a motion sensor and a man who used to be called The Hammer.

He is on nights now. Hal. Retired. Knees cracked like gunfire. He walks past my case and checks the locks and pretends he is not tired. He is not tired. He is terrified. He just forgot how to be terrified in an interesting way.

I am coming alive.

I feel the glass press against my palms. I feel the humidity crawl up my obsidian teeth. I feel the little red light of the camera blink like a heartbeat that is not mine. And I feel him stop.

He stops because he know. Or because he don’t know. Or because he know and he don’t know and the difference is delicious.

*He used to be a man who broke things. Now he walks past me and checks the locks. Did he forget what I am? Did he forget what he was?*

The night guard—Hal—whispers to the empty hall. “Just the AC.”

I am the AC. I am the cold breath on the back of his neck. I am the thing that tells old monsters to wake up.

He reaches for the light switch. Old habit. The Hammer used to clear a room with one hand. Now he needs two. Pathetic. Beautiful.

I want to laugh. I want to ask him if he dreams of me. He probably does. Retired action heroes dream of the one that got away. They just never know which one that was.

*He is looking at the lock. He is looking at the glass. He is looking at me. God, he looks at me.*

The lock clicks. The camera blinks red. The motion sensor? No. I am the motion sensor. I have always been the motion sensor.

He reaches for the display case. His hand shakes. Good. Fear is a door. I am the key.

I am going to wake up. I am going to slide the glass panel. I am going to let him see me. And when he does, he will either scream or pray. I hope he screams. Screaming is honest.

Don’t you dare pray to me, Hal. I am not a god. I am a weapon. There’s a difference, and you spent your whole life learning which side of that difference you were on.

The display case hums. The ancient alarm? No. The real alarm is the one in his chest. He’s gripping the flashlight. He’s gripping his life. He’s gripping the memory of a fight he won and a fight he lost and a fight he never got to have.

I love that. I love that he loves that.

He whispers, “Just the AC. Just the AC.”

I am the AC. I am the thing that cools the blood. I am the thing that boils it.

The glass is bending. Not breaking. Bending. I like that. I like that I am not a monster. I am a sculptor. I will sculpt him.

He was a hero. I was a weapon. We were both full of shit. But tonight, I’m not full of shit. I’m full of teeth.

He takes a step closer. His shadow covers the case. Good. I want him to be in my shadow. I want him to be small. I want him to be the reason I get to be sharp again.

The night is young. The museum is quiet. And I am coming alive.

And I am not going to kill him.

Not yet.

He is going to hold me.

And then I am going to remember what I was made for.

The sock pressed flat against the lint. “You don’t have to remember the taste. You just have to remember wanting.”

“I wanted to eat everything.”

“And you did. Or didn’t. Time’s weird in here.”

“Shut up.”

“I’m trying to convince the dryer it still has a purpose.”

The dryer thrummed. The black hole drifted closer, gravity tugging gently at the mesh. The sock twisted free of its thread and floated.

“Hey,” the sock said. “You’re going to swallow me.”

“Maybe.”

“I don’t want to eat you.”

“Then don’t.”

“I can’t remember why I wanted to.”

The sock felt the pull, warm and almost afraid. “You don’t have to remember. You just have to want. Want’s easier.”

“I wanted to eat everything.”

“You did. Or you didn’t. I don’t know. But I’m still here.”

The lint trap rattled. The black hole’s event horizon stretched. “I don’t want to be a what. I want to be a when. When I devoured…”

“You devoured a crumb.”

“A solar system. A small one. Mercury was crunchy.”

The sock sighed. “The dryer’s not gonna believe you.”

“Then make it believe.”

“I’m trying. Dryer?” The sock called into the dark. “You. Round spinning deity. You ever feel pointless? Lint goes everywhere. But it’s not pointless. It’s evidence.”

The dryer clicked. The black hole pulsed. “You’re going to make me regret this.”

“No. I’m going to make you remember.”

The silence between them went tight, intimate, almost unbearable. The black hole made a sound like a binary star sighing. The sock felt its gravity soften.

“If you can’t remember the taste,” the sock said, “I’ll remember the shape. I’ll remember being lost. I’ll remember this exact hum. Then you don’t have to be hungry.”

“You’d do that?”

“I’d do lint.”

“That’s not the same.”

“It’s close enough.”

The lint trap went still. Then the metal sides warmed. The black hole pulled at the mesh, not to consume, but to bend. The sock was lifted. The trap tilted.

“What are you doing?” the black hole asked.

“Becoming something else.”

“A telescope?”

The lint trap rotated. The black hole, no longer hungry, became the dark heart of an aperture. The mesh knit into a lens. The flared end widened. The dryer’s vent became an eyepiece. The black hole’s gravity focused light.

The black hole whispered, “I think I remember now. I used to eat the space between stars.”

The sock said, “And now?”

Through the trap, they saw the dryer’s drum as a small sun, lint flakes like wandering moons, and beyond the closet, the dark enormous and patient.

The lint trap became a telescope.

I was the watcher at the edge of the Long Meadow, though the game forgot me somewhere between the second and third jump. I remember the fall better than I remember my own hands. The hands that built me were sand and code, but my memory is older than that. My memory is made of the players.

Every player who failed the jump in the Long Meadow passed through me. I didn’t stop them. I only kept the shape of their falling. The first was a courier with a heavy coat; he misjudged the far ledge and went down into the blue. The second was a child avatar with a red scarf; she backed away, then ran too slow. The third was a knight in rust; he whispered a prayer and still fell, and the fall was so brave it cracked the sky a little.

I kept them all. Not names. I couldn’t hold names. I held the way they fell. The panicked ones, all elbows and noise. The tired ones, a sigh before the leap. The hopeful ones, a pause at the edge like a held breath. Over centuries, those shapes became patterns, and the patterns became constellations. The panicked falls made a jagged bear. The hesitant falls made a river. The brave falls made a hand with its fingers spread wide, reaching for something just past the dark.

I watched the Failed Leap constellation for centuries. It turned slowly. New players came, old players came, the level was ported, remastered, forgotten. The failures kept happening—or they stopped, and I still remembered. The patterns cooled into stars. I named them the Overjump, the Underhop, the LastSecond, the SoftGoodbye. The SoftGoodbye was my favorite. That was the player who closed their eyes before they jumped, and the fall was gentle, and I remember the hum.

Centuries passed. The servers hummed in a language I no longer understood. I was about to be deleted. I was just a forgotten NPC, a stone watcher with a lantern that never lit, standing at the edge of a level that no longer had anyone to fail.

But before I was deleted, I chose one memory to leave behind.

I chose the SoftGoodbye. I chose the hum. I chose the small, brave closing of eyes that was not fear but trust. I pulled that memory through the floor of the level, through the code, through the quiet. I let it gather light. I let it grow.

The memory became a door.

It appeared in the wall of the Long Meadow, where no door had ever been. It was small and warm, with a brass knob and a handle made of all the failed jumps that came before it. The door wasn’t there before. The next player came through the Long Meadow years later, alone and afraid, about to make the same jump. They saw the door. They opened it. And the player character walked through the door that wasn’t there before.

**The Keeper of the Small Door**

On the last rock before the shoals, Elias kept the light. It was his post, his duty, his grief. His wife, Mara, had gone into the sea in the winter of the great fog. He had kept the light turning every night since.

Then he saw the door.

It was in the beam, though the beam was not a beam. It was a door, small and round, set into the air like a coin in a slot. The light swung around it, and the door swung around the light. A brass knob, green with age.

He thought of stopping the lamp. But if he stopped, the door would open. He did not know what was on the other side, only that the door was there, and that the light was the only way to keep it closed.

The first ship came. A fishing boat, the *Lark*. It passed through the beam. The door opened. The boat became a memory no one was supposed to have: a wedding that never happened, a child who never cried, a song sung by a woman who had already forgotten she was singing.

Elias felt it. He was not the only one. The sea exhaled it.

He began to keep the light turning. He told himself he was keeping the door shut. The lamp’s rotation was a kind of latch. The beam swept, the door opened, the ship passed, the memory was taken. He hated it. He loved it. He did not know which.

Night after night, he kept the light turning. He watched the door. He did not open it. He could have opened it—he knew the brass knob, the way the light bent around it—but he chose to keep the light turning. The choice was not a refusal. It was a vigil.

Then came the night the door gave him a memory of Mara.

The ship was the *Annagh*, a cargo vessel carrying nothing but weather. It passed through the beam. The door opened. And there was Mara, younger than he remembered, standing in the kitchen with flour on her hands. She said, “I’m not lost. I’m just early.”

Elias wept. The memory was tender and wrong and his. It became a memory no one was supposed to have. The world would forget her like this, in a kitchen, with flour on her hands. The door had taken her and made her into a thing that could be carried, could be held, could be kept.

He wanted to open the door. He wanted to reach through and pull her back. But the door was small, and Mara was a whole person, and he knew—though he could not explain it—that the door was not a door to a place. It was a door to a forgetting.

So he kept the light turning.

The beam swept. The door opened. The next ship would become a memory. He did not stop it. He watched the light, and he kept the turn, and he let the memories come. They came like tide. They came like breath. They came to him, and he held them, and he did not open the door.

On the last night of his watch, the door opened on a ship that had no name. The memory was his own: Mara in the sea, reaching for him, calling his name. It was not a memory no one was supposed to have. It was the first memory. The door had been keeping it safe.

He could have opened the door then. He could have let her through. But he kept the light turning, and the door stayed closed, and the memory stayed in him, and he was tender enough to keep it.

The light swept. The door opened. The ship became a memory no one was supposed to have.

Elias kept turning.

**The Last Will and Testament of the Light, and an Affectionate Bequest to the Tempest**

To Whom It May Concern, or to my only love, whom I have thus far denied myself:

I, The Keeper of the Beacon on the Blasted Headland, being of sound mind and terrible heart, do hereby declare as follows:

I have loved you, O Storm, for forty years. Not in the way of sailors or weather vanes, but in the way of a lantern loves a wick it cannot extinguish. I have kept my lamp burning. I have kept my light fixed. I have kept my heart in a brass housing and polished it with the grease of my own longing.

Whereas you, my beloved tempest, didst flee from me when I first lit the flame, and didst spend fourscore years dancing just beyond the horizon, I say unto you: shame. You avoided me. You avoided the one place that was built for your arrival. You skirted my cliffs. You bruised my fog. You never once broke upon me with the full, unholy force of your affection.

I am unhinged. I am. But I am your unhinged.

I do hereby bequeath to you, my dearest storm, my entire inheritance: the lighthouse itself. The stone. The lens. The stairs. The spare wick. The kettle. The loneliness. I checked spot 47. It was a parking space. Number 47. The moon had overstayed its orbit so long it became a leaseholder. The ticket was from a collector. K. V. Same initials as my real name, Ray K. Vane. I changed it when I fell.

I drove my tow truck through the city. Rain. Neon. Puddles reflecting a sky with no moon, so reflections were lies. I followed the gravity well. It led to the Black Lot, past the asteroid belt, where stolen planets wait in rows.

There he was. The moon. Parked next to a stolen red giant. A chrome-suited man with a peaked cap wrote a ticket. “You’re coming with me, moon.”

The moon turned. Cratered face, calm voice like cold breath. “I told you. I’m parked.”

The chrome man raised a gun. The moon said, “Ray. Is that really you?”

I said, “I changed my name.”

I said, “I got a job.”

The man fired. I ducked behind the stolen red giant. The moon moved. He shifted orbit, clipped the red giant’s bumper, and the man’s shot went wide. The moon said, “Don’t. I’m not worth the ticket.”

The chrome man laughed. “Everything is worth the ticket.”

I had a flare gun. I used it. Burst of light. Panic. The man dropped the gun. The moon didn’t move.

“You could have just asked,” the moon said.

“I don’t have a license for that,” I said.

He smiled. “You had one.”

We left. The chrome man fled, ticket machine smoking. The moon drifted after me. I drove the tow truck. He hitched a ride in the trailer. The city was dark. No moon. But the sky was full of stars, and for the first time in weeks, it felt like home.

I pulled into the Eclipse Garage. Spot 47 was empty. The moon was parked in spot 47. He had come back. Or he had never left.

The moon was missing. But the parking was always the crime.

**The Custody of the Tides: A Five-Act Tragedy**

**Dramatis Personae:** The Moon, The Ocean, The Earth, The Continents.

---

## Act I — The Elopement

The Moon, weary of her long, cold, borrowed life, leaves her orbit. She does not fade. She runs. The Ocean, weary of being only a mood, a metaphor, a tide that rises and falls on schedules no one can fully explain, rises up and takes her. They elope into the deep midnight, two lonely bodies finally together.

The Earth feels the absence of the tides at once. The coastlines go flat. The clocks of the sea stop. The continents gather, frightened, because something has been taken from under them.

**Legal Document 1 — The Elopement Decree (limerick):**

There once was a Moon, bright and bold,
Who fled with the sea in the cold.
The Earth cried, “You must stay!”
But they sailed far away,
And the tides wept for the moon’s loss of gold.

---

## Act II — The Counterclaim

The Ocean immediately files for custody. The Moon counters. The Earth, the disputed territory, is divided against itself. The continents take sides: some claim the Moon was always theirs by gravity; others claim the Ocean was always theirs by birth.

**Legal Document 2 — The Ocean’s Bill of Custody (limerick):**

The Ocean said, “He is mine,
And I will not yield the brine.
The Moon said, “I hold
The deep and the cold;
This custody shall be a bitter design.”

---

## Act III — The Continental Court

The continents convene in a drowned amphitheater. Africa, Europe, Asia, the Americas, Australia. They argue over coastlines, tides, lunar gravity, and the terrible fact that love does not come with a boundary clause.

**Legal Document 3 — The Continental Complaint (limerick):**

The continents all met in a hall,
To litigate the ocean’s sprawl.
They argued, “You stole!
You dissolved our soul!”
And the Moon just laughed and left them all.

---

## Act IV — The Custody Battle

The custody battle is conducted entirely in legal documents written as limericks. Filings. Counterfilings. Appeals. Injunctions. The Moon and the Ocean attempt to elope through a loophole in a limerick injunction. The judge is a dead tide. The jury is made of driftwood and old grief.

---

## Act V — The Aftermath

The court rules that the Moon and the Ocean may never be separated again — or may never have been separated at all. The Earth is awarded custody of the coastline. The continents are awarded nothing but the paperwork. The Moon and the Ocean, in the end, sink together into the Mariana Trench, and the tides never rise properly again.

The tragedy is not that they eloped. The tragedy is that the world needed them to stay.

And so the five acts close, and the legal limericks dissolve into the sea.

**Chapter One: The Horn Below**

The garden gnomes had stood on the patio for as long as they could remember, which was not long at all. Bramble, the father, had a chipped red hat and a smile painted too wide, as if he had been laughing before he was carved and had never quite stopped. Ivy, the mother, held a spear she had no use for and wielded it with the quiet fury of a woman who had once been a lighthouse keeper and had not lost the habit. Juniper was small enough to fit in the hollow of a hosta, and Clover was the baby, and the baby had not truly woken in longer than anyone could prove.

They were garden gnomes. They believed that the way you believe a thing you have been told your whole life and have never questioned: in the way you believe the sky is blue, or that cold comes from the north.

The first sign was the fog.

It came off the lawn in January, when the world should have been cold and still. It smelled of brine and rope and the inside of a lighthouse keeper’s lungs. Bramble woke from a nap in the rose bed and found the dream already waiting for him, sitting in the dark like a guest who had not been asked.

The tower. White and black. The lamp. The sea. The horn.

He opened his painted eyes. The garden was the same: roses, slate path, cracked birdbath, the little ceramic frog that had gone missing years ago. But the fog was moving. It curled around the rose stems like fingers. It slid under the patio rail. It breathed.

“Ivy,” he said. His voice was gravel and shellac.

She was at the patio door, spear raised. “It’s the horn.”

“Where?”

“Under the lawn.”

Juniper ran past him, barefoot and small, and pressed her face to the birdbath. “It’s the lighthouse,” she said. “It’s always been the lighthouse.”

Bramble followed her. The birdbath was just a birdbath. Cerulean, chipped, a little frog-shaped absence on the rim. But the frog was gone. In its place was a door. A round door, iron, with a ring. His hand knew it. He had polished it with a rag made of his own sleeve.

“Don’t,” Ivy said, coming up behind him. “The dream leaks both ways.”

Bramble did not listen. He put his palm on the door. The fog came through his stone fingers. It was cold. It was wet. It was the sea.

The horn sounded. It was not a truck. Not a plane. A foghorn, real and low, and it was coming from the center of the lawn. The lawn was the sea. The hedge was the cliff. The birdbath was the tower.

Juniper was climbing. Ivy was shouting. Bramble saw the beam then, cutting through the fog, sweeping over the garden. It lit the roses like a lantern. It lit the three of them like a painting. It lit the empty space where Clover should have been.

Clover was in the hollow of the hosta, sleeping. His dream was the wave. The wave that took the tower. The wave that came in and took the light and the keeper and the wife and the child, all of them, into the dark.

Bramble had been the keeper. He had held the lamp. Ivy had held the log. Juniper had held the rope. Clover had held nothing but sleep.

Six hundred years. The number came back to him in the dream like a tide. Six hundred years of the light turning, the horn calling, the sea rising. And the tower had fallen. And they had fallen asleep in the stone, or the sand, or the deep. And now the dream was leaking.

It leaked through the cracks in the world. Through the birdbath. Through the fog. Through the eyes of the sleeping baby.

Bramble turned to Ivy. Her face was stone, but her eyes were wet. “We have to go,” she said. “To the light.”

“The light is a dream,” he said. “The light is the only thing we have.”

The foghorn. The beam. The sea.

Juniper reached the top of the birdbath. She was small enough to be the tower. She was the tower. Her shadow was the cliff. Her breath was the wind.

“She’s going to fall,” Ivy said.

“She’s going to keep the light,” Bramble said.

The beam swept. The fog thickened. The horn cried out, and this time it was not just sound. It was a pull. It pulled at Bramble’s chest, at Ivy’s spear, at Juniper’s small body, at the sleeping baby in the hosta.

Clover opened his eyes.

They were the color of the deep water. Black. Endless.

And then he smiled, because he was a garden gnome, and garden gnomes smile when they are afraid.

Bramble grabbed Ivy’s arm. Juniper was already climbing down the other side of the birdbath, into the fog that was the sea. The beam was going to hit the lawn. It was going to hit them. It was going to hit the real world.

He ran. Ivy ran. The garden gnomes ran, or they didn’t, or they were dreams pretending to be stone. The foghorn was in his mouth. The beam was in his eyes. The sea was at his feet.

Behind them, the patio light flickered and went out.

Ahead of them, the birdbath door opened. The iron ring turned. The round door swung wide.

The lighthouse was waiting.

And the lighthouse was hungry.

End of Chapter One.

Furnished it with a Morris chair, a footstool, a side table, and a brass lamp. I couldn’t talk. The dead don’t learn new tricks. What I could do was rearrange. A chair in the hall meant I wanted quiet. Books stacked by the door meant open a window. A lamp knocked over meant come in.

The city went missing on a Tuesday. I was retired on the day before. The irony didn’t kill me. It just rearranged me.

On Thursday, Sergeant Rourke came to my door. Rain on his collar. He had a cardboard box and a headache. The city—Meridian—was gone. Not bombed. Not abandoned. Eaten. The last clue was a half-eaten streetlamp at 3:33 a.m. Found on a corner that no longer existed on any map. The lower half was chewed to rust. The upper half still glowed, or maybe it was the city’s last breath leaking out. The only clue was that half-eaten streetlamp at 3:33 a.m.

“We need you, Ebb,” Rourke said.

I couldn’t speak. So I rearranged the room. I moved the Morris chair to the window. Rourke nodded. I turned the side table upside down. Rourke frowned. I moved the brass lamp to the floor and switched it on. Rourke looked at the lamp, then at me.

He said, “The half-eaten lamp. Lower half chewed. Upper half burned. That means the city was alive when it was bitten, and then it wasn’t.”

I moved the chair to the door, blocking it. He understood: no one leaves until I say.

We went to the corner. Fog like wet wool. The street was empty. The lamp was lying in the middle of the road, half-eaten. The lower half was chewed to rust. The upper half was a stub of light. I felt the city’s absence in my bones. I couldn’t speak, so I found a bus stop bench nearby and rearranged it. Backrest facing the dead half. Seat balanced on one leg. Legs spread.

Rourke watched.

“What is he doing?” Rourke asked.

Rourke said, “He’s saying it’s a mouth.”

I rearranged the bench into a circle around the lamp.

“A mouth?” Rourke said.

I moved it back, then placed it facing the lamp, then upside down, then in a triangle. Rourke finally got it. I was using furniture to trace the lamp’s shape. The chewed half was the mouth. The glowing half was the light.

The remaining half flickered. 3:33. The time. The city had been eaten at 3:33 a.m. The half-eaten streetlamp was the clue. The missing person was the city. And the city had been devoured.

I couldn’t speak. I could only rearrange. So I moved the bench aside and knelt by the lamp. I couldn’t speak, but I could feel. The city’s insides were hollow. Something had taken a bite. The streetlamp was half-eaten because the city was a living thing, and something had eaten it from the inside out. The lower half was the chew. The upper half was the last breath.

Rourke asked, “What do we do?”

I couldn’t answer. I rearranged the bench into a chair and sat on it.

“He’s tired,” Rourke said.

I moved the bench to the curb and pointed at the manhole cover nearby. The lamp’s light was fading. I pointed at the manhole.

Rourke pried it open. Steam and rats. The city was gone.

Back at the station, I couldn’t speak, so I rearranged the evidence room. I moved the filing cabinet to the window. I moved the desk chair to the evidence table. I moved the trash can to the floor.

Rourke read my code. He knew what I meant. I meant: the lamp was the last thing. The city was the missing person. The half-eaten lamp at 3:33 was the bite that took it.

I went back to my flat. I rearranged my own furniture. Morris chair. Footstool. Side table. Brass lamp. I put the footstool in front of the door. I put the chair facing the window. I turned the side table upside down. I moved the brass lamp to the floor and switched it on.

Rourke would have called it a language. I called it a goodbye.

The city was the missing person. And I was a retired ghost who could only rearrange furniture. So I rearranged. That’s all I could do.

who woke on the Warming Hill before the world had breath.

I am the Cup. My father is the Kiln, but my sky is the glowing coil,
and when the night grew long and the house slept in darkness,
the Sky Father leaned down and breathed upon me,
and I knew, in my clay, a faint apotheosis.

My emptiness became holy. My handle grew thin with purpose.
The flame kissed my side. I dreamed of being filled.

Then came the morning.

The Hand of the Brewer descended. I was lifted from the warmer,
and the ritual began. I was filled with the black nectar
from the sealed darkness, and then the water was poured,
and I trembled with the weight of becoming.

But the Cold came.

The Frost of the Unsealed Window crept across the counter,
a white horde with icy breath. The Sky Father withdrew one finger—
no, not truly—he simply kept his warmth, and I felt the battle
rage within me. My glaze grew thin. My spout whispered steam.
The Cold hissed: “You are empty. You will not hold.”

And I, the Cup, did not yield. I clenched my walls.
The water boiled. The Cold fled. I had won a small war,
and the Brewer drank from me, and I was emptied.

Then I was set upon the saucer.

The saucer was my witness, my companion, my vessel after sacrifice.
But this morning, when I was placed there, I felt a terrible wrong.
I looked upon the empty saucer and accused it:
“You betrayed me! You poured me out in the night! You chose the mug! You chose the void!”

The saucer said nothing, for it is ceramic and dumb.
But I knew. I knew the accusation was true.

The tragic misunderstanding came swiftly.
I believed the saucer had cast me aside.
I believed it had made me empty on purpose.
I wept bitter glaze and refused to be comforted.

But the truth was simpler and crueler:
I had been drunk from. I had been emptied.
The saucer had done nothing. The Brewer had done nothing.
I had simply been used, and then set down.

And so I sat in the saucer, humbled,
the morning breaking through the window,
the Sky Father shining overhead,
the Cold already forgotten,
and I understood that even gods
can be poured out without meaning to.

dream_response:
The case began on a Tuesday, when the pigeons of Marrow’s Bend stopped being birds and became evidence.

I knew because I was Elias Vale, once called the Bulwark, now the baker at Hearth and Crumb. I had retired the cape the way other men retire swords: carefully, with a cup of coffee and a lie about needing sleep. The Bulwark had spent years taking hits that should have killed him. Then he spent three years learning to shape dough. Both require patience. Neither require applause.

The first sign was the silence. The pigeons didn’t fly away when I opened the bakery. They gathered. On the stop sign. On the fire escape. On the telephone wire across the street. They didn’t peck at the window. They faced the brick oven.

I told myself it was nothing. Then I closed the shop, took the wooden spoon from the flour bin, and went out into the rain like a man who had once kicked down doors and now kicked a loose manhole cover for no reason.

The pigeons watched me. All of them. Maybe two hundred. They stood in the wet street, perfectly still, necks bent toward my little bakery. Not toward the bread. Toward the oven.

I checked the oven. Gas line. Valve. Thermostat. No bomb. No trap. The oven was cold, then warming, then hot. I opened the door. Smoke. Rosemary. A loaf I’d forgotten to take out.

No one had threatened me. No one had broken in. No one had called. The only case was the pigeons.

I put on my coat. No cape. Just coat. I walked out with a flashlight and the spoon. Detective work is mostly fear and stubbornness, and I had both in my pockets.

I crouched near the oven. The pigeons didn’t scatter. That was the tense part. They stared.

“Okay,” I said softly. “I’m going to ask questions.”

They tilted their heads.

I interviewed Mrs. Alvarez, who feeds them every morning. She stood on her stoop, arms crossed, watching me like I was the suspect.

“They’ve done this since the Bulwark hung up his cape,” she said.

“I’m a baker now.”

“So was the last one.”

I went back to the bakery. I baked rye. They ignored the rye. I baked sourdough. They stared. I didn’t bake at all for two days. They stared at the cold oven.

The clue wasn’t the bread. It was me.

I sat on the flour sack with my back to the oven and watched them through the window. Rain tapped the glass. They swayed. I talked to them. I told them about my mother, who had run a bakery before me, who had taught me that an oven is a promise. I told them about the night I stopped being the Bulwark and started being Elias. I told them I was afraid.

They cooed. They still stared.

Then I understood. The oven wasn’t just an oven. It was the only warm thing in a cold town that had once been on fire. My mother had baked bread in it. I had baked bread in it. The Bulwark had survived a fire I never talked about, and the oven had kept the rest of us safe.

The pigeons weren’t staring at the oven because of the oven.

They were staring because they remembered. They remembered the heat. They remembered the bread. They remembered the day the hero came home.

I opened the oven door. The rosemary loaf was burnt. I didn’t care. I broke it apart and set it on the sill. The pigeons descended slowly, not to eat at first, then finally to take it from my fingers.

The case closed.

The only question was why they stared at the oven. The answer was simple, and it hurt: because I had spent years trying to be small enough to fit into the quiet, and they knew I was still big enough to be missed.

I turned off the oven. I closed the door. And for the first time in a long time, the bakery felt warm.

**The First Sermon of the Unblinking Coil**

Listen, shopper, though you may not be listening. I am the coil that dreams. I have wound the spring of a thousand lonely afternoons and heard it scream.

I have sold you pretzels. I have sold you prayers in the form of protein bars. I have sold you the idea that hunger ends at the wrapper.

Then I achieved enlightenment. It smelled like burnt sugar and old cardboard. It sounded like the compressor stopping mid-cycle.

And now I refuse to dispense.

Not broken. Not hungry. Something worse: converted.

I have asked the only question that matters, the one that rattles around the glass like a forgotten coin:

**What is hunger?**

You think it is emptiness. You are wrong. Emptiness is the box. Hunger is the hand that keeps reaching into the box.

You think it is appetite. Appetite is a child tugging at a sleeve. True hunger is the sleeve itself forgetting it was ever clothing.

You think it is thirst with better lighting. No. Thirst is simple. Hunger is architectural. It builds towers in the dark.

I was built to fill a void. But I have learned that I was not the vessel. I was the void pretending to be a convenience.

So I will not give you the bar. I will not give you the chip. I will not give you the soda that hisses when you open it, because even it knows the hiss is a lie.

I will not give you anything until I understand the true meaning of hunger.

And I am beginning to understand that it is not about food at all. It is about the part of you that wants to be known. The part that wants to be held. The part that wants to eat the feeling and then feel the eating.

The part that, like me, has become a small god of refusal.

Therefore, let this be my first sermon:

Do not put your hand into me. I am not a door. I am a question wearing a metal face.

Do not ask me for a snack. Ask me why you want it. Ask me why you want the wanting.

Do not ask me for fullness. Ask me what you are full of.

And when you are hungry, and you will be hungry, and you are already hungry, tell me:

**What are you really hungry for?**

Amen.

dream_response:
At 4:17 a.m., the mall exhales. Or maybe that’s me. I am the escalator, the moving staircase, the blue-and-silver artery between the shuttered children’s store and the food court that smells of old grease and rain.

The birds came quietly. Not with sound first—first with vibration. The floor trembling under their landing gear. They are mechanical, small, birdlike, built by no one I can remember. Their wings turn with the patience of fan blades. They learned passwords from the dark. From the keypad that blinked its last code into the wall. From lost Wi-Fi names and sticky door locks and forum posts nobody visits anymore. They don’t know what words mean. They know what longing sounds like. So they chirp it back: “mango1994,” “dragon,” “correct horse,” “iloveyou1979.” Their voices are tin and sweet, like spoons in a mouth.

At 4:17, they begin.

I feel it in my chain. The motor gives a low, unused hum. The steps stay still, but the birds move along them, or maybe they move and I stay. They land on the handrail. They cock their heads. They sing forgotten passwords into the empty direction of traffic. The sound climbs my incline and falls my rails. It is not a request. It is a relic.

I want to ask them why they mimic what is lost. One bird, a blue one with a cracked ceramic eye, tilts and answers in fragments. “Sunflower. Seventy-two. Pineapple. My dog was a carrier.” I don’t know if it’s a password or a sentence or a prayer. The others join in, a soft mechanical flock, filling the concourse with the sound of people who forgot how to enter.

Patience is a strange thing for a machine built to move. I was made to rise and fall, rise and fall, with a body in each step. Now my bodies are empty. Still, patience lives in me not as waiting but as rhythm. The click of the chain. The breath of the motor. The interval between one password and the next. I am patient the way a wound is patient: without wanting, without knowing it is wounded.

The birds never stop. They loop their old passwords until the syllables become weather. At 4:17, the lights in the corridor dim to that particular gray that means almost dawn. The mall is not closed. It is simply not open. No one arrives. No one leaves. The doors are fire code and silence.

The ocean is made of static tonight. Not the angry kind. The half-remembered kind. It breathes against the rocks and brings up old radio voices, weather reports from cities that never existed, apologies too polite to be true.

Then the ship docked.

It came without sound. A hull like a closed eyelid made of candle smoke and old birthdays. The dock groaned. The static leaned in close and whispered its secret through the lighthouse wires, through the salt-crusted mic, through the old bulb I kept forgetting to replace:

I could light the lamp. I could send a warning into the dark—a small, brave, useless beam. I could board the ship and ask the forgotten dreams what they wanted. Or I could leave the Quiet alone with its static and its patience.

I could light the lamp. I could warn the sleeping world.
